claim: LINE-1/L1 retrotransposon sequences comprise 17% of the human genome.
source: LINE-1/L1 retrotransposon sequences comprise 17% of the human genome.
evidence: This is a well-established fact cited in the introduction with reference to Lander et al., 2001.

claim: L1 is the only autonomous retrotransposon that still drives human genomic plasticity today.
source: Among the many classes of mobile genetic elements, L1 is the only autonomous retrotransposon that still drives human genomic plasticity today.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about retrotransposons.

claim: L1 retrotransposition peaks during the S phase of the cell cycle.
source: Using functional, biochemical, and imaging approaches, we also show a clear cell cycle bias for L1 retrotransposition that peaks during the S phase.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by multiple experimental approaches shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: ORF1p enters the nucleus during mitosis.
source: Through imaging, genetic and biochemical approaches, we show that L1 nuclear import as well as L1 retrotransposition has a strong cell cycle bias (Figure 10). We also show that ORF1p and L1mRNA, probably in a complex with ORF2p, enters the nucleus during mitosis, accumulating in cells in the G1 phase (Figure 2).
evidence: This conclusion is supported by immunofluorescence data showing nuclear ORF1p in G1 cells (Figure 2) and proximity analysis (Figure 1C).

claim: ORF1p was detected in virtually all cells (≅ 97%) expressing ORFeus.
source: As previously observed (Taylor et al., 2013), ORFeus ORF1p was detected in virtually all the cells (≅ 97%) whereas ORF2p, encoded by the same bicistronic L1 mRNA also expressing ORF1p, was detected in just a subset of cells (≅10% using a rabbit anti-Flag antibody and ≅20% using a more sensitive mouse anti-Flag antibody) (Figure 1B, bar graph and inset).
evidence: This is quantified from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ORF2p was detected in just a subset of cells (≅10% using a rabbit anti-Flag antibody and ≅20% using a more sensitive mouse anti-Flag antibody).
source: As previously observed (Taylor et al., 2013), ORFeus ORF1p was detected in virtually all the cells (≅ 97%) whereas ORF2p, encoded by the same bicistronic L1 mRNA also expressing ORF1p, was detected in just a subset of cells (≅10% using a rabbit anti-Flag antibody and ≅20% using a more sensitive mouse anti-Flag antibody) (Figure 1B, bar graph and inset).
evidence: This is quantified from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Only 44% of cells displayed ORF1p expression when non-recoded L1 was over-expressed.
source: Interestingly, when non-recoded L1 was over-expressed, only 44% of cells displayed ORF1p expression.
evidence: This is quantified from immunofluorescence experiments comparing ORFeus and L1rp expression.

claim: Approximately 26% of cells showed clear nuclear ORF1p staining.
source: ORF1p was mainly present in the cytoplasm but some cells (≅26%) also showed clear nuclear staining (Figure 1A, Figure 1D, white arrowheads, Figure 1—figure supplements 1,2, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is quantified from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cells with nuclear ORF1p were usually observed as pairs of cells in close proximity.
source: Interestingly, the cells with nuclear ORF1p fluorescence were usually observed as pairs of cells in close proximity.
evidence: This observation is supported by proximity analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cells with nuclear ORF1p are statistically closer to each other than cells expressing ORF1p exclusively in the cytoplasm.
source: This 'proximity analysis', described in more details in the methods section, clearly shows that cells with nuclear ORF1p are statistically closer to each other than cells expressing ORF1p exclusively in the cytoplasm (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative proximity analysis with p=4.351e−13 shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ORF1p is nuclear in cells expressing Cdt1 (G1 phase).
source: Co-staining of ORF1p with geminin and Cdt1 clearly showed that ORF1p is nuclear in cells expressing Cdt1 (G1 phase), and completely cytoplasmic in cells expressing geminin (Figure 2A and quantification in B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence co-staining experiments shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: ORF1p is completely cytoplasmic in cells expressing geminin.
source: Co-staining of ORF1p with geminin and Cdt1 clearly showed that ORF1p is nuclear in cells expressing Cdt1 (G1 phase), and completely cytoplasmic in cells expressing geminin (Figure 2A and quantification in B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence co-staining experiments shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: No instances of cells with nuclear ORF1p-Halo and green nucleus (cells in S/G2/M) were observed in HeLa.S-FUCCI cells.
source: In this setting, no instances of cells with nuclear ORF1p-Halo and green nucleus (cells in S/G2/M) were observed (total number of cells counted = 3309; cells with nuclear ORF1p and green nuclei = 0; cells with nuclear ORF1p and red nuclei = 80).
evidence: This is quantified from live cell imaging of FUCCI cells shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ORF2p expression is not cell cycle regulated.
source: ORF2p-Halo was expressed in cells scattered throughout the cell cycle that displayed either orange (Cdt1 expressing) or green (geminin expressing) nuclei (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). This result suggests that ORF2p expression is not cell cycle regulated.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ORF2p is found in cells at different cell cycle stages.

claim: Nuclear signal of L1 mRNA was particularly bright in cells exiting mitosis identified by cytoplasmic bridges still connecting the two daughter cells.
source: Interestingly, and in line with our results on ORF1p localization (Figure 1C and Figure 2), nuclear signal of L1 mRNA was particularly bright in cells exiting mitosis identified by cytoplasmic bridges still connecting the two daughter cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is observed in RNA-FISH experiments shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: Nuclear L1 mRNA co-localized with cells with low Geminin and higher Cdt1 staining.
source: As shown for ORF1p and in line with our hypothesis, nuclear L1 mRNA co-localized with cells with low Geminin and higher Cdt1 staining.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-FISH combined with cell cycle marker staining shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: The percentage of cells with nuclear ORF1p does not increase but actually decreases after 48 hr of L1 induction compared to the 24 hr time point.
source: The analysis of ORF1p nuclear and cytoplasmic distribution surprisingly showed that the percentage of cells with nuclear ORF1p does not increase but actually decreases after 48 hr of L1 induction compared to the 24 hr time point (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is quantified from automated image analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Nuclear ORF1p is either degraded and/or exported from the nucleus during or after G1 phase.
source: The absence of an increase of cells with nuclear ORF1p with increased time of L1 induction, suggests that, after entering the nucleus in M phase, nuclear ORF1p is either degraded and/or exported from the nucleus during or after G1 phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nuclear ORF1p does not accumulate over time despite continued expression.

claim: An increased number of cells with nuclear ORF1p was observed after leptomycin treatment.
source: At both leptomycin concentrations, and using any of the Abs recognizing ORF1p we observed an increased number of cells with nuclear ORF1p after leptomycin treatment, suggesting that at least a subset of ORF1p is exported from the nucleus in a CRM1-dependent manner (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence quantification after leptomycin treatment shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: At least a subset of ORF1p is exported from the nucleus in a CRM1-dependent manner.
source: At both leptomycin concentrations, and using any of the Abs recognizing ORF1p we observed an increased number of cells with nuclear ORF1p after leptomycin treatment, suggesting that at least a subset of ORF1p is exported from the nucleus in a CRM1-dependent manner (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of leptomycin, a CRM1 inhibitor, on ORF1p localization.

claim: Increased time of nocodazole treatment fails to increase the percentage of M phase green cells.
source: Increased time of nocodazole treatment, and therefore longer time in M phase, fails to increase the percentage of M phase green cells (Figure 5A–B), suggesting that L1 retrotransposition does not occur during M phase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by retrotransposition assays with nocodazole treatment shown in Figure 5B.

claim: L1 retrotransposition does not occur during M phase.
source: Increased time of nocodazole treatment, and therefore longer time in M phase, fails to increase the percentage of M phase green cells (Figure 5A–B), suggesting that L1 retrotransposition does not occur during M phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of increase in retrotransposition with prolonged M phase arrest.

claim: Cells treated with thymidine showed no increase in GFP positive cells compared to untreated cells.
source: As with nocodazole treatments, cells treated with thymidine, showed no increase in GFP positive cells compared to untreated cells, suggesting that L1 does not preferentially retrotranspose in late G1 phase (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by retrotransposition assays with thymidine treatment shown in Figure 5C.

claim: L1 does not preferentially retrotranspose in late G1 phase.
source: As with nocodazole treatments, cells treated with thymidine, showed no increase in GFP positive cells compared to untreated cells, suggesting that L1 does not preferentially retrotranspose in late G1 phase (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of increase in retrotransposition with G1 arrest by thymidine.

claim: Mimosine treatment decreased L1 retrotransposition.
source: Mimosine treatments, also did not increase retrotransposition but actually decreased L1 hopping (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by retrotransposition assays with mimosine treatment shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Mimosine inhibits L1 retrotransposition not only by arresting the cell cycle but probably through additional metabolic mechanisms.
source: Our data showing a decreased retrotransposition in cells treated with mimosine, suggest that mimosine inhibits L1 retrotransposition not only arresting the cell cycle but probably through additional (metabolic?) mechanisms (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mimosine decreases retrotransposition more than expected from cell cycle arrest alone.

claim: A peak of retrotransposition was identified in the S phase in synchronized cells.
source: This approach allowed us to identify a peak of retrotransposition in the S phase (Figure 6E top and bottom left panels).
evidence: This is demonstrated by measuring retrotransposition at different time points after synchronization, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Control non-synchronized cells showed a linear increase in retrotransposition and no clear peaks.
source: Control non-synchronized cells, as expected, showed a linear increase in retrotransposition and no clear peaks were identified (Figure 6F top, bottom right panels).
evidence: This is demonstrated by measuring retrotransposition in unsynchronized cells shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The average conversion time from blue to red fluorescent timer is 2.35 ± 0.52 hr.
source: Our quantification also supports the previously reported timing of FT maturation (Subach et al., 2009) with an average conversion time from blue to red of 2.35 ± 0.52 hr (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is quantified from live cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 50% of cells expressed visible GFP at 2.71 ± 0.46 hr after doxycycline induction.
source: Quantification of cells expressing GFP under control of a Tet CMV-inducible promoter revealed that 50% of the cells expressed visible GFP at 2.71 ± 0.46 hr and 90% of the cells expressed visible GFP within 8.01 ± 0.63 hr of doxycycline treatment (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is quantified from live cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 90% of cells expressed visible GFP within 8.01 ± 0.63 hr of doxycycline treatment.
source: Quantification of cells expressing GFP under control of a Tet CMV-inducible promoter revealed that 50% of the cells expressed visible GFP at 2.71 ± 0.46 hr and 90% of the cells expressed visible GFP within 8.01 ± 0.63 hr of doxycycline treatment (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is quantified from live cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Analysis of 'blue only' sorted cells revealed a strong enrichment in S phase cells, a partial enrichment in cells in the G2/M phase and a strong de-enrichment of cells in G1 phase.
source: Analysis of the cell cycle stage of FACS sorted 'blue only' cells (cells that underwent retrotransposition within about 3 hr of the analysis, also considering the time needed for transcription of the marker) compared to fluorescence negative cells FACS sorted from the same population (cells that did not undergo retrotransposition before analysis) revealed a strong enrichment in S phase cells, a partial enrichment in cells in the G2/M phase and a strong de-enrichment of cells in G1 phase (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS sorting and cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Blue+ cells with lower red fluorescence are mainly in S phase (G1 = 9.38%, S = 78.1%, G2/M = 12.5%).
source: Consistent with the previous experiments, the blue+ cells with lower red fluorescence (blue peak) are mainly in S phase (G1 = 9.38%, S = 78.1%, G2/M = 12.5%).
evidence: This is quantified from SYTO61 staining and flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Blue+ cells with higher red fluorescence were mainly in G2/M phase (G1 = 0%, S = 10.9%, G2/M = 89.1%).
source: Blue+ cells with higher red fluorescence (purple peak), which had more time to proceed through the cell cycle after retrotransposition and before analysis (from S to G2/M), were mainly in G2/M phase (G1 = 0%, S = 10.9%, G2/M = 89.1%).
evidence: This is quantified from SYTO61 staining and flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: ORF2p was recruited on chromatin in S phase in a similar manner to Upf1 and PCNA.
source: Supporting our previous results, ORF2p was recruited on chromatin in S phase in a similar manner to Upf1 and PCNA (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by chromatin fractionation and western blot analysis shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: The PCNA-ORF2p complex is mainly chromatin bound.
source: The PCNA-ORF2p complex is mainly chromatin bound (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), supporting the idea that PCNA binds ORF2p during retrotransposition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fractionation and immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several MCM proteins (MCM3, MCM5 and MCM6) as well as TOP1, PARP1 and RPA1 were identified as ORF2p/PCNA interactors.
source: Among the identified ORF2p/PCNA interactors (279 from the first experiment and 158 from the second experiment) we identified several MCM proteins (MCM3, MCM5 and MCM6) as well as TOP1 (DNA topoisomerase 1), PARP1 (Poly [ADP-ribose] polymerase 1) and RPA1 (Replication Protein A1) (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequential immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of ORF2p pulled down L1 mRNA.
source: As expected, IP of ORF2p pulled down L1mRNA (Figure 9D, top panel) as well as direct IP of PCNA also showed interaction of this protein with the L1 mRNA (Figure 9D, top panel) compared to control IPs performed using normal mouse IgG antibodies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by IP-RT-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Direct IP of PCNA showed interaction of this protein with the L1 mRNA.
source: As expected, IP of ORF2p pulled down L1mRNA (Figure 9D, top panel) as well as direct IP of PCNA also showed interaction of this protein with the L1 mRNA (Figure 9D, top panel) compared to control IPs performed using normal mouse IgG antibodies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by IP-RT-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Sequential IP of ORF2p followed by PCNA IP pulled down L1 mRNA.
source: In line with our hypothesis that the ORF2p-PCNA complex is potentially retrotransposing, sequential IP of ORF2p followed by PCNA IP also pulled down L1 mRNA (Figure 9D, lower panel) compared to control IgG IP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequential IP-RT-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 9D.

claim: A subset of nuclear ORF2p puncta overlapped with PCNA foci in cells synchronized in S phase.
source: Finally, we performed immunofluorescence staining of ORF2p and PCNA in HeLa cells synchronized in S phase by double thymidine synchronization. A subset of nuclear ORF2p puncta overlapped with PCNA foci, marking potential regions of active DNA replication (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence co-staining shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Chromatin bound and retrotransposition-competent L1 particles are depleted of ORF1p and mainly consist of ORF2p in complex with L1 mRNA and host factors involved in retrotransposition.
source: Overall, these data suggest that chromatin bound and retrotransposition-competent L1 particles are depleted of ORF1p and mainly consist of ORF2p in complex with L1 mRNA and host factors involved in retrotransposition.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple observations including ORF1p export, differential antibody recognition, and lack of ORF1p interaction with PCNA/MCM6.

claim: The full length, active L1 retrotransposons consists of a 5' untranslated region (UTR) containing a bidirectional promoter (Speek, 2001; Swergold, 1990), two open reading frames (ORFs), ORF1 and ORF2, separated by a short inter-ORF region and a 3' UTR with a weak polyadenylation signal (Doucet et al., 2015; Dombroski et al., 1991; Burns and Boeke, 2012; Burns, 2017).
source: The full length, active L1 retrotransposons consists of a 5' untranslated region (UTR) containing a bidirectional promoter (Speek, 2001; Swergold, 1990), two open reading frames (ORFs), ORF1 and ORF2, separated by a short inter-ORF region and a 3' UTR with a weak polyadenylation signal (Doucet et al., 2015; Dombroski et al., 1991; Burns and Boeke, 2012; Burns, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about L1 structure supported by multiple citations.

claim: A short, primate specific, third ORF of unknown function called ORF0 was described in the 5'UTR of L1 with an antisense orientation compared to ORF1 and ORF2 (Denli et al., 2015).
source: A short, primate specific, third ORF of unknown function called ORF0 was also described in the 5'UTR of L1 with an antisense orientation compared to ORF1 and ORF2 (Denli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Denli et al., 2015.

claim: LINE-1 exhibits 'cis-preference' (Wei et al., 2001).
source: LINE-1 exhibits 'cis-preference' (Wei et al., 2001), the mechanism of which is unknown.
evidence: This is cited from Wei et al., 2001.

claim: ORF1p is an RNA binding protein with chaperone activity (Martin and Bushman, 2001; Khazina et al., 2011).
source: ORF1p is an RNA binding protein with chaperone activity (Martin and Bushman, 2001; Khazina et al., 2011) while ORF2p contains domains with endonuclease (EN) and reverse transcriptase (RT) activity (Feng et al., 1996; Mathias et al., 1991; Weichenrieder et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Martin and Bushman, 2001 and Khazina et al., 2011.

claim: ORF2p contains domains with endonuclease (EN) and reverse transcriptase (RT) activity (Feng et al., 1996; Mathias et al., 1991; Weichenrieder et al., 2004).
source: ORF1p is an RNA binding protein with chaperone activity (Martin and Bushman, 2001; Khazina et al., 2011) while ORF2p contains domains with endonuclease (EN) and reverse transcriptase (RT) activity (Feng et al., 1996; Mathias et al., 1991; Weichenrieder et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Feng et al., 1996; Mathias et al., 1991; Weichenrieder et al., 2004.

claim: Ribonucleoprotein particles (RNPs), consisting of many ORF1p molecules, as few as one or two ORF2ps and one L1 mRNA (Khazina et al., 2011; Basame et al., 2006; Dai et al., 2014) form in the cytoplasm.
source: It is believed that ribonucleoprotein particles (RNPs), consisting of many ORF1p molecules, as few as one or two ORF2ps and one L1 mRNA (Khazina et al., 2011; Basame et al., 2006; Dai et al., 2014) form in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is cited from Khazina et al., 2011; Basame et al., 2006; Dai et al., 2014.

claim: L1 RNPs accumulate in cytoplasmic stress granules (SGs) and processing bodies (PBs) (Goodier et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2015; Doucet et al., 2010).
source: L1 RNPs accumulate in cytoplasmic stress granules (SGs) and processing bodies (PBs) (Goodier et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2015; Doucet et al., 2010), but the role of these cellular structures in the L1 lifecycle is still controversial.
evidence: This is cited from Goodier et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2015; Doucet et al., 2010.

claim: Nuclear ORF1p was observed in a certain percentage of cells using cell lines and cancer specimens (Sokolowski et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2016; Doucet et al., 2016; Goodier et al., 2007; Harris et al., 2010).
source: L1 RNPs accumulate mainly in the cytoplasm but nuclear ORF1p was also observed in a certain percentage of cells using cell lines and cancer specimens (Sokolowski et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2016; Doucet et al., 2016; Goodier et al., 2007; Harris et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Sokolowski et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2016; Doucet et al., 2016; Goodier et al., 2007; Harris et al., 2010.

claim: L1 endonuclease nicks the DNA at A/T rich consensus target sites (5'-TTTT/AA-3') (Feng et al., 1996).
source: In the nucleus, L1 endonuclease nicks the DNA at A/T rich consensus target sites (5'-TTTT/AA-3') (Feng et al., 1996) and through a process called TPRT (Target Primed Reverse Transcription)(Cost et al., 2002; Luan et al., 1993) inserts a DNA copy into the new genomic target locus.
evidence: This is cited from Feng et al., 1996.

claim: Progression through the cell cycle was shown by several groups to promote L1 retrotransposition (Shi et al., 2007; Xie et al., 2013).
source: Progression through the cell cycle was shown by several groups to promote L1 retrotransposition (Shi et al., 2007; Xie et al., 2013) but a molecular understanding of this aspect has been elusive.
evidence: This is cited from Shi et al., 2007; Xie et al., 2013.

claim: It has been proposed that nuclear breakdown during mitosis could represent an opportunity for entrance of L1 into the nucleus (Xie et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2007).
source: Because of the importance of the cell cycle in efficient retrotransposition, it has been proposed that, as for some exogenous retroviruses (Goff, 2007; Suzuki and Craigie, 2007), nuclear breakdown during mitosis could represent an opportunity for entrance of L1 into the nucleus (Xie et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Xie et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2007.

claim: Effective retrotransposition was demonstrated in non-dividing and terminally differentiated cells (Kubo et al., 2006; Macia et al., 2017).
source: This hypothesis, never directly tested previously, was challenged by studies demonstrating effective retrotransposition in non-dividing and terminally differentiated cells (Kubo et al., 2006; Macia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Kubo et al., 2006; Macia et al., 2017.
